pages.text: Root Cause Analysis
pages.sourceText: Root Cause Analysis

pages.text:
General process for performing root cause analysis
1.
Define the problem. 
2.
Gather data/evidence. 
3.
Identify issues that contributed to the problem. 
4.
Find root causes. Identify which causes to remove or change to prevent repeated 
problem.
5.
Develop solution recommendations that effectively prevent repeating the problem.  
6.
Implement the recommendations / changes.
7.
Observe the recommended solutions/changes to ensure effectiveness of 
eliminating the problem.

pages.text:
7 Best Practices to remember
1 Your root cause analysis is only as good as the info you collect.
2 Your knowledge (or lack of it) can get in the way of a good root cause analysis.
3 You have to understand what happened before you can understand why it happened.
4 Interviews are not about asking questions.
5 You can’t solve all human performance problems with discipline, training, and procedures.
6 Often people can’t see effective corrective actions even if they can find the root cause.
7 All investigations do not need to be equal (but some steps can’t be skipped).

Objective: 
Use Fishbone analysis to identify the root causes of a high defect rate in a 
product manufactured by a company and suggest improvements.
Scenario
A company manufactures consumer electronics, and recently, there’s been an 
increase in defective products, leading to higher return rates and dissatisfied 
customers. Management has asked you to investigate the reasons for the high 
defect rate and propose corrective actions.
Exercise: Analyzing High Product Defect Rates

Choose the Right Tool:

Problem: Two coworkers disagree about which software to use.
• If the deadline is tomorrow: Use Compromising ("Let’s pick 
one and adjust later").
• If you need both ideas to succeed: Use Collaborating ("Let’s 
combine the best features of both").
• If it’s not urgent: Use Avoiding ("Let’s talk about it next week").
•
It’s all about picking the best way to handle each situation!

pages.text:
Tips in conflict management
1.
Conflict is normal, there is tension in all relationships.
2.
Remember that you're on the same team, not opposing factions.
3.
Never assume malice, just ignorance/misunderstanding.
4.
Refuse to escalate. Start a calm baseline and never escalate from there, even if the 
other party escalates their emotions drastically.

Case Study: Transforming Business Reporting Through Data Automation
Background:
The current reporting process at company XYZ is time-consuming and error-prone, 
involving several employees copying data from spreadsheets. You as a new business 
analyst, want to introduce an automated data dashboard system using Power BI to 
streamline reporting and provide real-time insights. However, the proposal faced 
resistance:
•
Employees feared the system might replace their roles.
•
Managers were skeptical about the reliability of automation.
•
Stakeholders were disengaged, doubting whether the change was worth the effort.
Use the 6 principles of persuasion to navigate the issues
